title: Memory in the Gym
bigQuestion: How have empire, occupation, slavery and injury shaped whom martial arts communities choose to honor, and how can a historian tell that story factually?

story.title: A Photograph Above a Flag
story.kicker: A wall of honors is also a set of choices.
paragraphs: In a practice hall, a black-and-white photograph of a founder hangs high on the front wall. Below it hangs a national flag. The founder in the photograph grew up under a different government and never trained under that flag. A visitor asks why the two hang together.

The owner explains that the photograph honors a teacher and the flag honors the country where the art now lives. Both choices are real, and both are recent. Someone decided which picture to frame, which flag to hang and which names to leave off the wall.

Martial arts grew up amid empires, occupations and wars. Okinawa was a kingdom before Japan annexed it in 1879. Korea was a Japanese colony from 1910 to 1945. Capoeira grew among enslaved Africans in Brazil. These histories shape how gyms remember their pasts.

Historians read a wall of honors the way they read any document. They ask who made it, when, and for whom. They also look for people the wall leaves out, such as teachers from a colonized people or athletes who died after a bout.
story.think: What does a wall of photographs tell you about the people who hung it, and what might it leave out?

lessons.title: Karate Day in Okinawa
lessons.mainIdea: In 2005 Okinawa's prefectural assembly named October 25 Karate Day, marking the art as Okinawan heritage after a long history of annexation and occupation.
reading: Okinawa was the center of the Ryukyu Kingdom until Japan annexed it in 1879. After the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, the islands came under United States *administration*. They returned to Japanese rule on May 15, 1972. Large U.S. military bases remained afterward.

On October 25, 1936, a group of Okinawan karate teachers met in Naha. A local newspaper organized the meeting, and its record shows the teachers agreeing to write karate with characters meaning empty hand. In 2005 the Okinawa Prefectural Assembly chose that date for an annual *Karate Day*.

The choice is an act of *commemoration*. It ties karate to Okinawa, not to mainland Japan or to the many foreign schools the art later produced. Okinawan leaders have used the day to draw visitors and to argue that the islands are karate's home. The day is a memory claim built from a dated record.

words.d: government control over a territory, sometimes by an outside power
an act, such as a holiday or monument, that honors and remembers a past event
October 25, named by the Okinawa Prefectural Assembly in 2005 to honor karate's Okinawan roots

look.title: Choosing a Date
look.text: Okinawa could have marked many dates for karate: the 1879 annexation, the 1922 demonstration in Tokyo, or the 1972 return to Japan. The assembly chose October 25, the day of a 1936 meeting of Okinawan teachers in Naha.
look.prompt: Why might Okinawan leaders have chosen a meeting of Okinawan teachers rather than a date tied to Tokyo or to the U.S. period?

check.q: When did Okinawa return to Japanese rule after U.S. administration?
check.why: Okinawa returned to Japanese rule on May 15, 1972.

check.q: What does October 25 commemorate?
choices: A 1936 meeting of karate teachers in Naha
check.why: Karate Day marks the October 25, 1936 meeting in Naha.

check.q: Who named Karate Day in 2005?
check.why: The Okinawa Prefectural Assembly chose the date in 2005.

lessons.title: Hwarang and the Written Record
lessons.mainIdea: Early taekwondo histories linked the art to Silla's hwarang, but historians working from records show its modern roots in karate learned under colonial rule.
reading: The *hwarang* were groups of young aristocrats in the ancient Korean kingdom of Silla. The Samguk sagi, a Korean history completed in 1145, describes them. It tells of their loyalty, their travels to mountains and rivers, and their service in war. It does not describe an unarmed art named taekwondo.

In the decades after 1945, many official taekwondo books opened with the hwarang and with old paintings of fighting figures. This framing suited a newly independent nation. It pointed back to a Korean past and away from the colonial years when Japan ruled Korea.

Historians have tested that story against records. Udo Moenig's 2015 study traces early taekwondo to Korean founders who learned karate in Japan or under Japanese rule. The earliest kwan of the 1940s taught karate forms. Recognizing that *historiography* does not lessen the art; it shows how a nation remembered its past.

words.d: groups of young aristocrats in the ancient Korean kingdom of Silla, described in the Samguk sagi
the study of how history has been written, and why writers told it as they did
a history of Korea's Three Kingdoms, completed in 1145

look.title: A Historian on Taekwondo's Roots
look.text: Moenig argues that taekwondo's early forms and training came largely from Japanese karate, which Korean founders learned during the colonial period, and that later accounts stressing ancient Korean origins served national purposes.
look.cite: Udo Moenig, Taekwondo: From a Martial Art to a Martial Sport, Routledge, 2015
look.prompt: Does this argument say the hwarang did not exist? What exactly does it question?

check.q: When was the Samguk sagi completed?
check.why: The Samguk sagi, which describes the hwarang, was completed in 1145.

check.q: What is historiography?
choices: The study of how history has been written
check.why: Historiography asks how and why writers told history as they did.

check.q: What did Moenig's study trace early taekwondo to?
check.why: Moenig traced early taekwondo forms to karate learned during the colonial period.

lessons.title: Korean-Born Fighters in Japan
lessons.mainIdea: Some famous fighters in postwar Japan were born in Korea under colonial rule, and their Korean birth was often hidden or left out of public memory.
reading: Japan ruled Korea from 1910 to 1945. Hundreds of thousands of Koreans moved or were brought to Japan in those years for work. From 1940 a colonial policy pressed Koreans to take Japanese-style names. Many Korean families in Japan kept those names after the war to avoid *discrimination*.

Rikidōzan was born in Korea in 1924 and came to Japan as a young man. He wrestled in sumo, then became Japan's most famous professional wrestler in the 1950s, when his televised bouts drew huge crowds. During his lifetime, his Korean birth was little known to the Japanese public. He died in 1963.

Ōyama Masutatsu, the founder of Kyokushin karate, was also born in Korea during colonial rule. His Korean name was Choi Yeong-eui. Later biographies and Korean media brought both men's origins into the open. Their stories show how *identity* can be left off the wall of honor.

words.d: unfair treatment of people because of who they are, such as their national origin
who a person is, including family, birthplace, language and nation
government of one people by an outside power that has taken control of their land

look.title: Two Biographies
look.text: A 1950s Japanese magazine profile of a famous wrestler gives his hometown as a place in Japan. A biography published decades later names his birthplace in Korea and his Korean birth name.
look.prompt: Why might the two accounts differ? What would you check to decide which one is accurate?

check.q: From what year did colonial policy press Koreans to take Japanese-style names?
check.why: From 1940 the colonial government pressed Koreans to adopt Japanese-style names.

check.q: What was Ōyama Masutatsu's Korean name?
check.why: Ōyama was born in Korea as Choi Yeong-eui.

check.q: Why did many Korean families in Japan keep Japanese-style names after 1945?
choices: Because Korean names were banned in Korea
check.why: Many families kept the names to avoid discrimination in Japan.

lessons.title: Zumbi and November 20
lessons.mainIdea: Brazil honors Zumbi dos Palmares on November 20, and many capoeira groups remember him as a symbol of resistance to slavery.
reading: Palmares was a large *quilombo*, a community of people who escaped slavery, in the hills of northeastern Brazil. It lasted for most of the 1600s. Portuguese colonial forces attacked it many times. Its last leader, Zumbi, was killed on November 20, 1695.

In the 1970s, Black activists in Brazil chose November 20 to mark Black Consciousness Day. The date honored Zumbi rather than the 1888 Golden Law, which a princess had signed. Many states and cities made the day a holiday. In December 2023 a federal law made it a national holiday across Brazil.

Capoeira groups often join the day's events with public *rodas*. Many capoeira songs name Zumbi or Palmares. Teachers present capoeira as part of Afro-Brazilian history of resistance. The choice of hero shows a community remembering its past through its own leaders.

words.d: a community founded in Brazil by people who escaped slavery
the circle in which capoeira is played, with music and singing
Brazil's November 20 day honoring Zumbi and Afro-Brazilian history

look.title: Two Dates for Freedom
look.text: Brazil could mark the end of slavery on May 13, the day of the 1888 Golden Law signed by Princess Isabel. Many Afro-Brazilian groups instead mark November 20, the day Zumbi of Palmares was killed in 1695.
look.prompt: What does each date honor, and why might a capoeira group prefer one of them?

check.q: What was Palmares?
choices: A quilombo of people who escaped slavery
check.why: Palmares was a large quilombo in northeastern Brazil in the 1600s.

check.q: When did November 20 become a national holiday in Brazil?
choices: By a federal law of December 2023
check.why: A federal law of December 2023 made Black Consciousness Day a national holiday.

check.q: Why did activists choose November 20 instead of May 13?
choices: To honor Zumbi's resistance rather than a royal decree
Because the Golden Law never passed
check.why: November 20 honors Zumbi, a leader of resistance, not the princess who signed the law.

lessons.title: Mestre Pastinha's Last Years
lessons.mainIdea: Mestre Pastinha, who guarded Capoeira Angola, died poor in 1981, and his later honors show how memory can come after neglect.
reading: Vicente Ferreira Pastinha was born in Salvador, Bahia, in 1889. In 1941 he opened a center for Capoeira Angola, the older style of the game. He wrote about capoeira and taught for decades in the historic Pelourinho district. Visiting writers and musicians came to watch his *academy*.

In the early 1970s, Pastinha lost the use of his academy space during work on the old buildings of the Pelourinho. By then he was elderly and losing his sight. He lived his last years in poverty, far from the students who had once filled his hall. He died in Salvador in 1981, at the age of 92.

Later generations made Pastinha a central figure of Capoeira Angola. His photograph hangs in many Angola schools around the world. Brazil's heritage recognition of capoeira in 2008 honored the *mestres* who carried it. The contrast between his poverty and his fame is part of the honest record.

words.d: master; the title for a senior capoeira teacher
a school with a fixed place, teacher and program
the older style of capoeira, which Mestre Pastinha worked to keep

look.title: Honor After Neglect
look.text: A capoeira school in Chicago hangs a photograph of Mestre Pastinha in a white cap. Visitors see a revered teacher. The caption beneath notes that he died poor and nearly blind in Salvador in 1981.
look.prompt: Why might a school include the hard facts in the caption instead of showing only the honored image?

check.q: When did Pastinha open his Capoeira Angola center?
check.why: Pastinha opened his center in Salvador in 1941.

check.q: What happened to Pastinha's academy space in the early 1970s?
choices: He lost its use during work on the Pelourinho buildings
check.why: Work on the old Pelourinho buildings cost him his academy space.

check.q: What does mestre mean?
check.why: Mestre is the title for a senior capoeira teacher.

lessons.title: Jack Johnson's Pardon
lessons.mainIdea: Jack Johnson, the first Black heavyweight champion, was convicted in 1913 under a law used against him, and was pardoned after his death in 2018.
reading: Jack Johnson won boxing's world heavyweight title in 1908, the first Black man to hold it. Many white Americans reacted with open hostility. In 1913 a federal jury convicted him under the Mann Act of 1910. The law banned taking women across state lines for immoral purposes.

Historians describe the prosecution as racially motivated. It targeted Johnson's relationships with white women. Johnson left the country rather than go to prison. In 1920 he returned and served about a year in federal prison. He died in 1946 after a car crash in North Carolina.

For decades, boxers, historians and members of Congress asked for a *posthumous pardon*. President Donald Trump granted one on May 24, 2018. The *pardon* forgave the conviction; it could not undo the years Johnson lost. It shows a nation revising, through law, whom it honors.

words.d: an official act by a president or governor that forgives a crime
happening after a person has died
a 1910 federal law used to convict Jack Johnson in 1913

look.title: Dates in Jack Johnson's Record
look.cite: U.S. Department of Justice, clemency grant of May 24, 2018; federal court records of United States v. Johnson, 1913
look.prompt: How many years passed between Johnson's death and his pardon? What does that gap suggest about how memory changes?

check.q: When did Jack Johnson win the heavyweight title?
check.why: Johnson won the world heavyweight title in 1908.

check.q: What does posthumous mean?
check.why: Posthumous means after death; Johnson's pardon came 72 years after he died.

check.q: Under which law was Johnson convicted?
check.why: A federal jury convicted him under the Mann Act in 1913.

lessons.title: Foreign-Born Wrestlers in Sumo
lessons.mainIdea: Wrestlers born outside Japan rose to sumo's top ranks from 1972, and their success raised debate about who may hold Japan's national sport's highest honor.
reading: Sumo is run by the Japan Sumo Association and is closely tied to Shinto ritual and Japanese identity. For most of its professional history, its wrestlers were Japanese. Wrestlers from Hawaii began joining sumo stables in the 1960s. Takamiyama, born in Maui, won a top-division championship in 1972.

Konishiki, also from Hawaii, reached the second-highest rank, ōzeki, in 1987. In 1993 Akebono, born Chad Rowan in Hawaii, became the first foreign-born *yokozuna*, sumo's highest rank. Wrestlers from Mongolia followed. Asashōryū became yokozuna in 2003, and Hakuhō later set records for tournament wins.

Their rise sparked debate. The association limited each stable to one foreign-born wrestler, a *quota* it tightened in 2010 to count naturalized citizens. Supporters called the rule a way to keep sumo Japanese. Critics saw it as closing doors. The record shows both the openings and the limits.

words.d: the highest rank in professional sumo
a fixed limit on how many people of a group may take part
a sumo training house where wrestlers live and train under a master

look.title: Firsts for Foreign-Born Wrestlers
look.cite: Japan Sumo Association banzuke and tournament records
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first foreign-born top-division champion and the first foreign-born yokozuna?

check.q: Who became the first foreign-born yokozuna in 1993?
check.why: Akebono, born Chad Rowan in Hawaii, became yokozuna in 1993.

check.q: What is a quota?
choices: A fixed limit on how many of a group may take part
check.why: The association's rule set a quota of one foreign-born wrestler per stable.

check.q: What did the 2010 change to the stable rule do?
check.why: In 2010 the association tightened the rule to count naturalized citizens.

lessons.title: A Stone in Kamakura
lessons.mainIdea: A memorial to Funakoshi Gichin at Engaku-ji in Kamakura carries his saying that karate has no first attack, showing how students choose the words that represent a founder.
reading: Funakoshi Gichin, born in Shuri, Okinawa, in 1868, brought karate to mainland Japan in the 1920s. He died in Tokyo in 1957. His students later placed a *memorial* stone at Engaku-ji, a Zen Buddhist temple in Kamakura. Groups of his followers gather there in his memory.

The stone carries a saying linked to Funakoshi: karate ni sente nashi, often translated as there is no first attack in karate. It is one of twenty *precepts* credited to him. By choosing this line for the stone, his students set the founder's public image as a teacher of restraint.

A memorial stands at a place his students chose, in mainland Japan rather than Okinawa. It speaks in words they selected. Historians read such a monument as evidence of how a community wanted to remember a founder. They compare it with his books and the records of his life.

words.d: a stone, building or event made to remember a person
a short rule meant to guide conduct
a Zen Buddhist temple in Kamakura, Japan, where a memorial to Funakoshi stands

look.title: Choosing the Words
look.text: A founder wrote books, taught for decades and left many sayings. His students picked one line, there is no first attack in karate, to carve into stone at a temple in Kamakura.
look.prompt: What does choosing that line tell you about how his students wanted him remembered? What might a stone in Shuri have said instead?

check.q: Where is the memorial to Funakoshi described here?
check.why: The stone stands at Engaku-ji, a Zen temple in Kamakura.

check.q: What is a precept?
choices: A short rule meant to guide conduct
check.why: The saying on the stone is one of twenty precepts credited to Funakoshi.

check.q: How do historians read a memorial?
choices: As evidence of how a community wanted to remember someone
check.why: A monument shows the choices of the people who built it.

lessons.title: Duk Koo Kim, 1982
lessons.mainIdea: The death of Korean boxer Duk Koo Kim after a 1982 title bout led the WBC to shorten championship fights from 15 to 12 rounds.
reading: On November 13, 1982, Duk Koo Kim of South Korea fought Ray Mancini for a lightweight title in Las Vegas. The bout was scheduled for 15 rounds and was shown on national television. Kim was knocked out in the 14th round. He died from a brain injury four days later.

The death set off public debate about safety in boxing. The World Boxing Council, one of the sport's sanctioning bodies, soon shortened its title fights from 15 rounds to 12. Other major *sanctioning bodies* made the same change over the following years. Twelve rounds became the standard length for world title fights.

Kim's name is rarely on gym walls, yet his death changed the rules every champion since has followed. His mother and the referee of the bout both died by suicide within the following year. Historians tell such *tragedy* plainly, with dates and consequences, because it explains why the rules look as they do.

words.d: an organization that approves title fights and names champions in professional boxing
a very sad event, such as a death, that causes deep suffering
the World Boxing Council, a professional boxing sanctioning body

look.title: A Rule With a Name Behind It
look.text: A boxing program lists a world title bout scheduled for 12 rounds. Before 1982, the same program would have listed 15. The change is printed without any explanation.
look.prompt: Why might a historian argue that the number 12 is a kind of memorial? What does the program leave out?

check.q: Whom did Duk Koo Kim fight in November 1982?
check.why: Kim fought Ray Mancini for a lightweight title in Las Vegas.

check.q: What change did the WBC make after Kim's death?
choices: Shortened title fights from 15 to 12 rounds
check.why: The WBC cut title fights from 15 rounds to 12.

check.q: What is a sanctioning body?
choices: An organization that approves title fights and names champions
check.why: Sanctioning bodies like the WBC approve title fights and name champions.

lessons.title: Taekwondo Across a Border
lessons.mainIdea: In 2018 the two rival taekwondo federations performed together in South and North Korea, a rare meeting across the divided peninsula.
reading: Korea has been divided since 1945, and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953 ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty. Taekwondo divided too. South Korea backs World Taekwondo and Kukkiwon. North Korea hosts a branch of the ITF, the federation of Choi Hong-hi.

In February 2018, South Korea hosted the Winter Olympics in PyeongChang. North and South Korean athletes marched together at the opening ceremony. Around the Games, a World Taekwondo team and an ITF team from North Korea gave joint *demonstrations* in South Korea. In April 2018 the World Taekwondo team performed in Pyongyang.

The events did not merge the two federations. They showed that taekwondo carries the memory of a divided nation. Each side's version grew from the same postwar roots. A *reconciliation* on stage can honor that shared past without settling who owns the name.

words.d: a public performance to show a sport or art, not a scored contest
a coming together again after conflict
an agreement to stop fighting, which is not the same as a peace treaty

look.title: One Stage, Two Uniforms
look.text: In 2018 two taekwondo teams stood on one stage. One wore the uniform of World Taekwondo from South Korea. The other wore the uniform of the ITF from North Korea. Each team performed its own forms, and then they performed together.
look.prompt: What did a shared stage say about taekwondo's history that a single team could not?

check.q: Which Games did South Korea host in February 2018?
check.why: South Korea hosted the 2018 Winter Olympics in PyeongChang.

check.q: What is an armistice?
check.why: The Korean War ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty.

check.q: What did the 2018 joint demonstrations NOT do?
choices: Bring the teams onto one stage
check.why: The shows were joint performances; the federations stayed separate.
